Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

far adverb

by far, much

also by far, far better, far more, much better, easily (the best)

classical

Cic. de Or. 1.11: multō pauciōrēs ōrātōrēs (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 1.6: multō facilius atque expedītius iter (Lewis & Short)

multō

adverb

far, much (with comparatives)

multō melior, far better; with verbs of preferring, multō mālō, I’d much rather (Cic. Att. 12.21.1, Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • longē — by far (with superlatives)

    adverb · also used · classical · Hor. S. 1.5.89: pānis longē pulcherrimus; Ter. Ad. 1.1.40: errat longē (Lewis & Short)

    With comparatives longē is poetic and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short); classical prose says multō.

  • facile — easily, beyond question (with superlatives, prīmus, prīnceps)

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 6.10.2: ōrdinis tuī facile prīnceps; Cic. Rosc. Am. 15: ejus vīcīnitātis facile prīmus

    English “easily the best”. Lewis & Short: often in Cicero, rare elsewhere.

Examples

  • vēnit vīlissima rērum hīc aqua, sed pānis longē pulcherrimus

    here water, the cheapest thing there is, is sold for money; but the bread is by far the finestHor. S. 1.5.88–89

See also far, a lot, very.

SourcesLewis & Short: multo · Lewis & Short: longe · Lewis & Short: veneo · Lewis & Short: facilis (facile)

Cicero (Fam. 6.10.2, Rosc. Am. 15) checked against the Perseus Latin texts.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-horatius), checked against the editions named there. In Hor. S. 1.5.88 we write vēnit (from vēneō, is sold), as the metre requires; the collection has venit.
